@graph.name: tTG-IgA and Total IgA Tests
@graph.description: Tissue transglutaminase IgA (tTG-IgA, anti-TG2 IgA) with total serum IgA is the first-line blood-testing pair for suspected coeliac disease in people consuming gluten. Low IgA, prior gluten restriction and limited disease can produce false-negative serology. Confirmatory approaches vary by age, clinical setting and current guideline.

mainEntity.name: What is the tTG-IgA blood test?

acceptedAnswer.text: An antibody assay used as a first-line screen for coeliac disease in people eating gluten.

mainEntity.name: Why is total IgA tested with tTG-IgA?

acceptedAnswer.text: Total IgA identifies IgA deficiency that can make tTG-IgA falsely negative.

mainEntity.name: Can tTG-IgA diagnose coeliac disease alone?

acceptedAnswer.text: A high result is strongly informative, but confirmation depends on clinical context and guideline-based specialist assessment.

mainEntity.name: Is tTG-IgA the same as anti-TG2 IgA?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Both refer to IgA antibodies against tissue transglutaminase 2.

mainEntity.name: What symptoms suggest coeliac disease?

acceptedAnswer.text: Chronic diarrhoea, bloating, fatigue, weight loss, iron deficiency and some extraintestinal manifestations.

mainEntity.name: Can coeliac disease cause constipation?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. It does not always present with diarrhoea.

mainEntity.name: Can low iron or ferritin indicate coeliac disease?

acceptedAnswer.text: Unexplained iron deficiency is an important reason to consider coeliac testing.

mainEntity.name: Can coeliac disease cause osteoporosis?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Malabsorption and chronic inflammation can contribute to poor bone mineral density.

mainEntity.name: Does a negative tTG-IgA rule out coeliac disease?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Low total IgA, gluten restriction and some clinical phenotypes can cause negative serology.

mainEntity.name: Should I stop eating gluten before testing?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Remain on a gluten-containing diet until the clinician completes diagnostic assessment.

mainEntity.name: I already stopped gluten—can I still test?

acceptedAnswer.text: Tell your clinician. The antibody result may be falsely low, and specialist-supervised options may be needed.

mainEntity.name: What is selective IgA deficiency?

acceptedAnswer.text: A low or absent IgA state in which IgG-based coeliac assays are preferred for assessment.

mainEntity.name: What is DGP-IgG?

acceptedAnswer.text: An antibody to deamidated gliadin peptides used in certain situations, particularly IgA deficiency.

mainEntity.name: What is endomysial antibody (EMA)?

acceptedAnswer.text: A highly specific coeliac-related antibody assay often used to clarify selected cases or confirm high-titre pathways.

mainEntity.name: What does tTG-IgA more than 10 times normal mean?

acceptedAnswer.text: High titre can qualify selected patients for specialist-led no-biopsy diagnosis under recent guidance; it is not a universal self-diagnosis rule.

mainEntity.name: Do all adults need a duodenal biopsy?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Recent European and UK guidelines permit selected high-titre specialist pathways without biopsy; many adults still require biopsy.

mainEntity.name: What does a duodenal biopsy show?

acceptedAnswer.text: It can identify villous atrophy and related changes while allowing evaluation of other causes of malabsorption.

mainEntity.name: Can coeliac disease occur without digestive symptoms?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Anaemia, bone disease or autoimmune associations may be more prominent.

mainEntity.name: Is coeliac disease a wheat allergy?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Coeliac disease is autoimmune; wheat allergy is an IgE-mediated allergic condition.

mainEntity.name: Is gluten sensitivity the same as coeliac disease?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Non-coeliac gluten/wheat sensitivity is a separate diagnosis after appropriate exclusion of coeliac disease and wheat allergy.

mainEntity.name: Does an IgG food intolerance panel diagnose coeliac disease?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Standard IgG food panels are not validated for coeliac diagnosis.

mainEntity.name: Can a child have the tTG-IgA test?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, with age-specific clinical evaluation and paediatric gastroenterology pathways.

mainEntity.name: Should first-degree relatives be tested?

acceptedAnswer.text: Risk is higher in close relatives; discuss targeted testing with a clinician.

mainEntity.name: Is coeliac disease linked to type 1 diabetes?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Coeliac disease is more frequent in type 1 diabetes and sometimes prompts targeted evaluation.

mainEntity.name: Can liver tests be abnormal in coeliac disease?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Mild elevated transaminases can occur, although other causes must also be assessed.

mainEntity.name: Can a normal tTG after treatment prove intestinal healing?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Serology is useful for follow-up but cannot reliably confirm villous recovery.

mainEntity.name: How often should tTG be repeated after diagnosis?

acceptedAnswer.text: Follow the gastroenterologist’s plan and nutrition assessment; an arbitrary fixed interval is not appropriate for everyone.

mainEntity.name: Is fasting required for tTG-IgA?

acceptedAnswer.text: Fasting is generally not needed, but continuing gluten is important.

mainEntity.name: Can I interpret a positive result from the number alone?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The assay-specific upper limit, total IgA, diet and clinical picture are required.

mainEntity.name: Should I start a gluten-free diet after a positive screening result?

acceptedAnswer.text: Discuss confirmation first with the clinician; prematurely eliminating gluten can interfere with definitive assessment.
